title: Observability and Path Health

sections.title: Where a Request Can Be Observed

html:
A customer contacted Baodium support with a simple question: “Did my order go through?” They had clicked Place Order, watched the progress indicator for several seconds, and refreshed the page when no confirmation appeared. The refreshed page showed that the order was being processed, and a confirmation email arrived a few minutes later, but by then the customer could not tell whether the refresh had placed a second order.

The support agent found one order, and the on-call engineer found two authorization requests for it in the Payment Service logs, one that had timed out and one that had succeeded. The service dashboards showed normal CPU and memory usage, payment provider response times that had risen from about 400 milliseconds to more than a second, and checkout requests waiting longer than usual for database connections. The slow-query log showed nothing unusual, and no metric had crossed a paging threshold. None of these measurements connected the customer’s request to the payment attempts, the committed order, or the response the gateway sent back, so the engineer could not determine whether the customer had received confirmation that the order was complete or whether the card had been charged twice.

The earlier chapters introduced mechanisms for controlling dependency latency, preserving uncertain operations, and routing data reads. To operate those mechanisms, Baodium needed records that distinguished a completed business operation from a completed server response and a confirmation actually displayed to the customer. The investigation therefore moved from isolated service dashboards to measurements at each boundary of the checkout path.

Where a Request Can Be Observed

Follow one checkout from the customer’s browser to the order database and back again. The database can record that the order was committed. The gateway can record that it sent a response. The browser can record that it displayed a confirmation. Each record answers a different question.

Suppose the database commits the order and the gateway loses its connection before the response reaches the browser. The customer sees a spinner and may try again, although the order already exists. Or the gateway sends the response, but the customer closes the page before it appears. If we measure only completed server requests, we cannot tell these situations apart. We need observations at all three boundaries, and we must account for the ones we cannot confirm.

At the database, every change to an order or payment state also writes a row to a state-transition table within the same transaction. If the transaction rolls back, the row is rolled back with it, so any count derived from these rows matches what was committed. A counter incremented in application code after the commit cannot offer that guarantee, because the process could crash between the commit and the increment.

The gateway is the reverse proxy in front of every Baodium service, and it writes one access-log entry for each request when that request ends. Because every request passes through the gateway, the log also captures requests whose backend crashed and requests that the customer abandoned. For instance, Nginx logs status 499 when the client closes the connection before the response is sent, and the checkout gateway records those requests with a disconnected outcome. Each entry also records the route, HTTP status, duration, request identifier, and a protected reference to the operation, which we discuss later in the chapter.

In the browser, a short script sends a submission report when the customer places the order and a display report when a result appears on screen. Both reports include timestamps from the browser’s Performance API and are sent with navigator.sendBeacon, which asks the browser to deliver the report even if the page is closing. Delivery is still not guaranteed, because ad blockers, privacy settings, crashed tabs, and network failures all prevent some reports from arriving. For that reason, a checkout without a display report is counted as unknown rather than successful.

The gateway entry also defines a request’s server-side duration, which runs from the moment the gateway accepts an authenticated, well-formed request until it finishes the response or records that the request ended without one. Connection setup, TLS negotiation, and page rendering fall outside that interval, so they are visible only in the browser’s timing, as Figure Figure shows.

With all three records in place, comparing them shows where a checkout went wrong. For instance, a committed order paired with gateway status 499 shows that the client disconnected before the gateway finished sending its response; the gateway cannot establish what the browser displayed. A gateway response reporting a pending outcome, paired with a browser display report that still shows an indefinite progress indicator, indicates a separate page-rendering problem.

Metrics, Logs, and Distributed Traces

These observations require different records. Choosing between metrics, logs, and traces depends on the information each retains, its collection cost, and the questions an operator must answer during an incident. A metric is aggregated inside the service before it is sent. A request counter, for instance, takes the same space whether it counted ten requests or ten million, because only the running total leaves the process. In exchange, a metric cannot describe any individual request. A log record is written for every event, so it preserves the details of each request, but its volume, and with it its cost, grows with traffic. A trace records every step of a request as it passes through each service, so its cost grows with traffic multiplied by the number of steps, which is why most systems keep traces for only a sample of requests.

These trade-offs determine the order in which we use the three during an investigation. We start with metrics, because they count every request and can show whether something is wrong and which requests are affected. We then open traces for a few of the affected requests, because a trace is the only record that shows how a single request’s time was divided across services. Finally, we turn to logs for the details of individual events and for the identifiers that link a request to work that continued after it ended.

Telemetry Collection and Storage

Between the line of code that records a measurement and the graph an engineer opens during an incident, telemetry passes through a series of layers. Most organizations have the same layers, irrespective of the tools they use: instrumentation inside each service, collectors near each workload, a processing tier that filters, samples, and buffers data, a storage system for each kind of telemetry, and dashboards and alerting on top. At Baodium, the instrumentation is the OpenTelemetry SDK in every service, and collection is handled by an OpenTelemetry Collector agent on every host, together with Prometheus scraping for metrics. Processing happens in a pool of gateway collectors, Prometheus and Thanos store metrics, Loki stores logs, Tempo stores traces, and Grafana and Alertmanager provide dashboards and alerts. Three design decisions in this pipeline shape the rest of the chapter.

The first decision is how metrics travel from each service to the store. With the pull model, a scraper such as Prometheus fetches each service’s /metrics endpoint on a fixed schedule, every 15 seconds at Baodium. With the push model, each service sends its data to a collector on its own schedule. The two collection models expose different failure signals. If Prometheus cannot reach a service, it records a failed scrape, and we can alert on that failure. If a service that pushes its metrics fails, however, its data stops arriving, and an absence of data looks the same as a healthy service with nothing to report, which is why Baodium pulls its metrics. Traces and logs are pushed, but only as far as an agent collector on the same host. The SDK sends data to that agent in the background, so a slow or unavailable backend never delays a customer’s request.

The second decision is where to apply the rules that every service must follow. Baodium’s agents forward all telemetry to a central pool of gateway collectors, which remove known sensitive fields, add resource attributes, sample traces, and buffer data when a backend slows down. If each team implemented these rules in its own service, some services would omit them and others would run outdated versions. A central tier keeps the rules consistent, but it also creates a shared dependency, because a failure in the gateway pool affects the telemetry of every service at once.

The third decision is how to link the separate stores. Metrics, logs, and spans end up in three separate systems, so engineers need shared keys to navigate from one to another. OpenTelemetry attaches resource attributes, such as service.name, service.version, and the deployment region, to everything a service emits. Trace identifiers in log records connect logs to traces, and exemplars, which we discuss later in the chapter, connect histogram buckets to traces. With these keys in place, an engineer can select a slow point on a latency graph, open the trace behind it, and then view the logs written during that trace.

Service Health and Monitoring Coverage

When checkout failures increase, the initial health check establishes whether a required service is reachable and its instances are running. Baodium runs about forty services, each deployed as several instances, and every service has the same five kinds of monitoring.

Health endpoints.

Kubernetes checks two conditions on every instance, and the results lead to opposite actions. The liveness endpoint reports whether the process can do any work at all. After repeated liveness failures, Kubernetes restarts the container, because a restart is the only way to recover a process that is stuck. The readiness endpoint reports whether the instance should receive traffic at the moment. When readiness fails, Kubernetes stops routing requests to the instance but leaves it running, which suits an instance that is still starting up or is temporarily overloaded. Both checks should test only the instance itself. If a check also queried a shared database, a slow database would make the check fail on every instance at once, and Kubernetes would restart or remove all of them together, turning a slowdown into an outage.

Scrape status and inventory.

Kubernetes acts on failing health checks but does not alert anyone, so Baodium’s instance alerts come from Prometheus. For each instance it scrapes, Prometheus records a metric called up, which is 1 when the scrape succeeds and 0 when it fails. An alert on up == 0 that lasts two minutes detects an instance that has stopped responding. However, an instance that drops out of service discovery is no longer scraped at all, so its up series ends rather than falling to 0, and the alert has nothing to evaluate. Baodium closes this gap with three additional checks. An absent(up{job="order-service"}) rule fires when a critical service has no up series at all. A comparison between the number of scraped instances and the kube_deployment_status_replicas_available metric from kube-state-metrics detects instances that are running but not being scraped. Finally, a job that compares the service catalog with Prometheus’s targets every five minutes detects services that were never discovered.

Request metrics.

An instance can respond to every scrape and still fail every request it serves. For that reason, every service also exports the same three request metrics, known as RED: request rate, error rate, and duration. Together, these metrics describe what a caller experiences, namely how much work arrives, how much of it fails, and how long it takes. Because every service uses the same metric names, a single dashboard template covers all forty services.

External probes.

All of the checks so far run inside Baodium’s network, so they cannot detect a failure that occurs in front of it. If DNS stops resolving, a certificate expires, or the content delivery network fails, customers cannot reach checkout at all, while the services behind it see only a drop in traffic and report no errors. To detect failures of this kind, Baodium simulates customers from outside its network. Synthetic probes run every minute from three locations in separate regions, so that a network problem near one location is not mistaken for an outage. Some probes fetch the checkout page and verify its status code and certificate expiry date, some place a test order with a test card, and one looks up the status of a known test order.

Heartbeats.

Background workers need a check of their own, because they serve no requests and so produce no request metrics. A worker that is stuck in a loop or waiting on a lock also continues to pass its liveness check. A healthy worker, however, always makes progress, so progress is what we measure. Each worker records the time of its last successful run in a gauge, which is a metric that can decrease as well as increase, and an alert fires when time() - reconciliation_last_success_timestamp_seconds exceeds ten minutes.

Not every one of these alerts should page an engineer. When a single instance fails, the load balancer routes its traffic to the remaining instances and customers are unaffected, so the alert is sent to a ticket queue instead. During the incident, all five kinds of checks passed, which ruled out a failed service and led the engineer to examine measurements of the checkout itself.

Request Metrics and Latency Distributions

The engineer’s next question was whether the problem affected a single request or many. The checkout dashboard answers that question using two metrics emitted by the gateway, shown in Listing Listing: a counter, which only increases and counts requests, and a histogram, which records how long those requests took.

Labels and Cardinality

The names in braces are labels, and they make these metrics far more useful. Imagine standing in front of a full classroom and asking for “the student” to come forward. Nobody stands, because nobody knows whom you mean, but if you ask for Amaka, one person stands. A label serves the same purpose for a metric that a name serves in that classroom. Without labels, the request counter is a single number for the entire fleet, and a failure in one region, or in a new version running on 5 percent of instances, is lost in the total. With labels, every request is counted under its route, region, version, and outcome, so you can query exactly the subset of traffic you need.

The outcome label deserves closer attention. It takes five values, confirmed, rejected (for a business reason such as a payment decline), pending, failed, and disconnected, and together they reveal two common failures that average response time and HTTP error counts both miss, since neither failure produces an HTTP error. In the first, checkout responds quickly while a growing share of customers receive pending results instead of confirmations, which can even lower the average response time, because a pending response returns sooner than a confirmation. In the second, checkout confirms every order while customers wait well beyond the response target. Beside these panels, the dashboard shows the number of unresolved payment operations and the age of the oldest one, because a worker’s heartbeat shows only that reconciliation is running, not whether it is keeping up.

Label cardinality has a direct storage and memory cost. Each distinct combination of label values becomes its own time series, and the monitoring system maintains an index entry and an in-memory buffer for every series. As a result, cost grows with the number of combinations rather than with traffic, which is why each label must have a small, fixed set of values. For instance, a route label holding the template /orders/{order_id} has one value regardless of how many orders exist, whereas a route label holding the literal path /orders/ creates a new series for every order until the monitoring system runs out of memory. Order numbers and similar identifiers belong in logs and traces instead, because those systems are designed to look up individual records.

To see how quickly these combinations grow, suppose we added an instance label. Six regions, three versions, forty instances, and five outcomes produce 3,600 combinations. A classic Prometheus histogram with eight bucket limits stores eleven series for each combination (nine bucket series, including the implicit +Inf bucket, plus a sum and a count), which brings a single latency metric to 39,600 series. Baodium therefore limits checkout metrics to four labels and opens per-instance views only after those labels have narrowed down the problem.

Latency Histograms

A single latency figure hides what an engineer most needs to know, namely how many customers had a slow experience and how slow it was. An average blends the fast majority with the slow minority, so a small group of very slow requests barely changes it. Percentiles avoid this problem because they describe the shape of the distribution rather than its center. The median is the latency at or below which half of all requests fall, and the 99th percentile is the latency at or below which about 99 percent fall, which makes it a measure of the slowest 1 percent. During the incident, the median checkout latency in the affected region held at about 0.8 seconds, while the 99th percentile rose from about 2 seconds to about 6.5 seconds. This pattern told the engineer that the problem was severely affecting a small share of requests rather than slowing every request slightly.

You might expect each service to report its own 99th percentile, but percentiles cannot be combined across instances. If one instance reports 1 second and another reports 5 seconds, the fleet’s 99th percentile could fall almost anywhere between them, depending on how many requests each instance handled. Counts, by contrast, can be added, and a histogram takes advantage of that by recording latency as a set of counters called buckets, each counting the requests that finished within a given upper limit, and the percentile is calculated from the bucket counts summed across all instances.

The checkout histogram uses limits of 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, and 10 seconds. Because the 3-second limit matches the response target, the fraction of checkouts answered within target is an exact division of two counters rather than an estimate, as Listing Listing shows. In this and later PromQL listings, rate(…[5m]) converts each counter, which only ever increases, into a per-second rate over the last five minutes, and le="3" selects the 3-second bucket.

Any other percentile is an estimate, because the query engine interpolates within the bucket that contains it. Listing Listing sums the bucket counts across instances before estimating the percentile, which is the correct order of operations. You should also display the request count beside every percentile, because a 99th percentile computed from forty requests changes sharply whenever a single request is slow.

Because a histogram records a request only when it finishes, a request that hangs remains invisible until it times out. Two gauges cover this gap by tracking the number of checkout requests in progress and the age of the oldest one.

Distributed Tracing and Latency Diagnosis

The metrics had narrowed the problem to the slowest checkouts in one region. Because a metric aggregates many requests into one number, however, it cannot show where any single request spent its time. A distributed trace can, because it records the path of one request through every service it touches. A trace resembles the timing sheet for a relay race, in which every leg is timed and the legs together account for the whole race. Each leg is a span, which is a named operation with a start time, an end time, a parent, and attributes such as an attempt number. Unlike a leg in a relay race, however, a span can contain smaller spans. Each service sends its spans to a shared backend, which reassembles them into a tree using the trace identifier and parent identifier that every span includes.

The engineer reached a slow trace from the latency graph through an exemplar. When a metrics library records a request’s duration while a trace is active, it can attach that trace’s identifier to the histogram bucket in which the request falls. A point on the 99th-percentile graph then links directly to a real request. Because the exemplar is attached before the sampling decision described later in the chapter, the trace it points to may have been discarded, in which case the engineer opens another exemplar from the same bucket.

A trace is useful only if its spans separate the operations that matter. If a single span called database.lookup covers waiting for a connection, running the SQL, and fetching rows, a slow lookup reveals nothing about which step was slow. The checkout path therefore has a separate span for each kind of delay: waiting for a database connection, holding that connection, running each statement, each payment attempt, and each retry delay. Instrumentation libraries create most of these spans automatically. The two connection spans, however, usually have to be added by hand, as in Listing Listing, because database instrumentation starts its span only when a statement is sent and has no visibility into the application’s connection pool.

The first block measures how long pool.acquire waits for a free connection. The second block runs from the moment the connection is handed over until it is released, so every operation performed in between, including calls to other services, appears as a child of db.connection.held. When reading spans like these, keep in mind that an outbound HTTP span measures the call from the caller’s side, including connection setup and network transfer. A long client span records a slow call as observed by Payment Service, but attributing the delay to the provider requires the provider’s own timings or a comparison with other callers.

Connection Pool Wait and Occupancy

Figure Figure shows the trace that the engineer opened, with illustrative durations. It came from another customer’s checkout that completed normally, and its gateway span lasted 5.2 seconds. The request spent its first 1.8 seconds in db.connection.acquire. Once it had a connection, Order Service committed the acceptance record and called Payment Service while still holding that connection. The first authorization attempt timed out after 1.5 seconds, the retry policy waited 0.2 seconds, and a second attempt with the same idempotency key succeeded after 1.4 seconds. Recording the result, local processing, and sending the response took the final 0.3 seconds. Because Order Service released the connection just before responding, db.connection.held ends shortly before the gateway span.

This trace explained why the slow-query log had shown nothing unusual. Nearly all of the database-related time was spent in db.connection.acquire, before any statement ran, and a slow-query log records only statements that take a long time to execute.

The Payment Service call nested inside db.connection.held suggested a cause, but it did not prove one, because connections could also have been held by slow queries or by other requests sharing the pool. To distinguish between these explanations, the engineer compared the pool’s connection hold time with query duration and with provider latency. If slow queries had been responsible, hold time would have risen with query duration. Instead, it rose and fell with provider latency. Together with the trace, this comparison established the mechanism. Each checkout held a database connection for the entire payment call, so when the provider slowed down, connections remained busy for longer, and new checkouts had to wait for a free connection at the start of their own requests.

Span Timing and Critical-Path Analysis

A common mistake when reading a trace is to add up the span durations, which counts time more than once whenever spans are nested. In this trace, db.connection.held contains the Payment Service call, which in turn contains both provider attempts and the retry delay, so adding all of them counts some of that time three times. Parallel branches cause a similar error, because two operations that run at the same time can add up to more than the time the caller waited. A simple check catches both mistakes: if the span durations add up to more than the request’s total duration, some of the spans overlap.

The critical path consists of the operations whose dependencies determine the end-to-end request duration. Improving work outside that path may reduce resource consumption, but it does not shorten the observed request unless the critical path changes. In this trace, the critical path ran through the connection wait, the first attempt, the retry delay, and the second attempt, which is why the changes discussed later in the chapter target the connection wait and the retry. When a trace shows a gap between spans, the request may have been waiting for a thread, running code that has no spans, or starved of CPU, and a CPU profile of the service usually identifies which. Timestamps from separate hosts also require care, because a clock difference between machines can place a child span’s start before its parent’s.

OpenTelemetry Instrumentation

So far, we have assumed that these spans exist. Baodium produces them, along with its metrics and logs, using OpenTelemetry, an open standard divided into parts so that a library can be instrumented once and its telemetry sent to any backend. Application code calls the API, which does nothing until an SDK is installed. This separation lets library authors add instrumentation without forcing a particular backend on the applications that use their libraries. The SDK, configured when the service starts, samples, batches, and exports the data, and instrumentation libraries create spans automatically for common frameworks, such as HTTP servers and clients, gRPC, database drivers, and message queues.

Instrumentation libraries cover the frameworks they support, but they cannot capture business meaning, such as what a pending checkout is or why a payment attempt number matters. Teams therefore add those spans and attributes by hand and agree on shared attribute names, such as checkout.outcome, payment.attempt, and operation_ref. Without that agreement, the same fact would be recorded under several names, and every query would need to account for all of them.

Trace Context Propagation

For a trace to follow a request across services, each call must pass along the trace it belongs to and the span that made the call. OpenTelemetry uses the W3C Trace Context standard for this purpose, which places both values in a single header, shown in Listing Listing.

Reading from left to right, the header contains the format version (00), the 32-character trace identifier, the 16-character identifier of the calling span, and a flags field, in which 01 means that the caller sampled the trace. Client instrumentation injects this header into each outgoing request, and server instrumentation extracts it and makes the new span a child of the caller’s span.

Standard HTTP and gRPC libraries handle this automatically. When context is lost, the cause is usually either a hand-written client that never adds the header or a handoff to another thread. OpenTelemetry stores the active span in a context tied to the current thread or task, and a thread pool does not copy that context to its workers unless it is told to. In Python, for instance, asyncio.to_thread copies the context, whereas a bare ThreadPoolExecutor does not. In the tracing backend, the symptom is a trace that ends abruptly, followed by an unrelated trace that begins where the first one stopped.

Messages propagate context through their headers in the same way, but a consumer usually should not continue the producer’s trace. A reconciliation job that runs minutes after checkout would otherwise stretch the checkout trace from seconds to minutes. Instead, the consumer starts a new trace and adds a span link back to the producer’s span. At the edge of the system, a traceparent header from a public client is untrusted input. Accepting it would allow any client to choose its own trace identifiers or force every request to be recorded, and the companion baggage header would allow it to insert arbitrary data into internal telemetry. Baodium’s gateway therefore discards both headers on public requests and starts a new trace.

Correlating Requests and Operations

For the customer, placing the order was one action. Across the service boundary, it was a journey made up of several separate executions: the original submission, the refresh, and, for a checkout that ends in a pending state, a reconciliation job that may run minutes later. Each execution has its own trace, so following the whole customer journey requires identifiers at three levels. A request identifier names a single HTTP request, so a refresh or a status poll receives a new one. A trace identifier groups the spans of one execution. An operation identifier groups every attempt and recovery step that belongs to one business operation, such as one checkout or one payment authorization.

Only the operation identifier spans the whole journey, so it must exist before the first request is sent. Baodium generates it when the checkout page is rendered and places it in a hidden form field. When the customer refreshed the page, the browser resubmitted the same value in request B that it had sent in request A. Order Service stores the identifier with the acceptance record, Payment Service passes it to the provider as the idempotency key, and in telemetry it appears only in a protected form, operation_ref, which we discuss at the end of this section.

The same identifiers link browser reports to gateway records, although one complication arises. Because a refresh resubmits the same operation, the operation reference cannot pair a display report with a single request, and because browser and server clocks can be several seconds apart, timestamps cannot pair them reliably either. To solve this, the gateway adds its request identifier to every response in a Server-Timing header, which the page’s script reads through the Performance API and includes in the display report. Each display report then matches exactly one gateway entry, and browser coverage can be measured as the share of completed checkout responses that have a matching display report.

Logs tie these separate traces together, because a single log record can hold all three identifiers. Writing logs as structured JSON makes every field searchable, and OpenTelemetry’s logging integrations add the active trace and span identifiers automatically. Listing Listing shows the record for one payment attempt, in which retry_owner names the component that decides whether to retry.

Records like this remain useful long after they were written when event names are fixed strings that a query can find in every release, and when outcomes distinguish a timeout from a decline or an unavailable connection. Most importantly, an outcome should describe only the attempt that produced it. A timeout means that Payment Service stopped waiting, not that the provider did nothing, and in this incident that distinction determined the answer.

Incident Reconstruction

When the engineer searched the logs for the order’s operation_ref, the records from both of the customer’s requests were returned together. Sorting them by timestamp produced the timeline in Table Table, where op-1 stands for the customer’s operation.

The timeline first shows why the gateway’s duration and the services’ durations must be read separately. Request A’s gateway span ends at 4.5 seconds with a disconnected outcome, yet its service spans continue until 5.0 seconds, because the services learned that the browser had disconnected only when Order Service tried to write its response. The timeline also shows that the refresh did not create a second order, because Order Service matched request B’s operation identifier to the operation it had accepted at 2.1 seconds. Finally, it shows that the customer never saw a confirmation, because none was ever returned.

Whether the card had been charged twice could not be determined from Baodium’s records alone. The payment record showed one authorization, but it contained only what Payment Service had learned, and because attempt 1 had timed out, the provider might have authorized the card without Baodium ever receiving the response. The answer had to come from the provider, which treats requests with the same idempotency key as one operation for 24 hours. The provider had marked its response to attempt 2 as a replay of an existing authorization, which meant that attempt 1 had succeeded and only its response had been lost. A lookup through the provider’s API by the same key returned exactly one authorization.

The confirmation email was sent through a transactional outbox. Order Service wrote an outbox row in the same transaction as the confirmed order, so the order could not be confirmed without the email request being recorded, and no email request could exist for an order that was never confirmed. A relay process then published the row to the email queue and retried whenever publication failed. Because a relay that crashes after publishing but before marking the row as sent will publish it again after restarting, the email consumer discards duplicates using the row’s identifier.

Sensitive Data in Telemetry

Logs are read by many people and retained for weeks, so they should never contain addresses, card details, credentials, or request bodies, and any identifier that someone could guess needs protection. For this reason, the operation identifier appears in telemetry only as operation_ref, an HMAC-SHA256 of the identifier keyed with a secret from a key-management service. A plain SHA-256 hash would not protect it, because operation identifiers follow a predictable format, and anyone could hash every plausible value and compare the results. Because the key is what prevents that attack, only four components hold it: the gateway plugin, the browser-report endpoint, Order Service, and the support lookup tool. Order Service passes the reference downstream with the trace context, so other services can log it without ever holding the key. The key is rotated yearly, and the support tool keeps the previous key for the 14 days that logs remain searchable. Outside the checkout form and the services that handle the operation, the raw identifier is stored only in the operational database and sent only to the payment provider.

No single control can keep sensitive data out of telemetry, so Baodium layers several. Services log through typed event structures that accept only approved fields, which prevents most mistakes at the source. The collectors remove deny-listed attributes and scan for patterns such as card numbers, although pattern matching misses values embedded in JSON strings or exception messages. Access controls and short retention limit the damage when something does get through. Finally, a weekly test injects fake card numbers into staging requests and searches every backend for them, which verifies that the filters work.

Telemetry Cost and Sampling

Every layer of the pipeline consumes CPU, network bandwidth, or storage. Because each kind of telemetry grows for a separate reason, each needs its own controls.

Metrics.

Metric cost grows with the number of series, so the label rules described earlier provide most of the control. In addition, the gateway collectors drop any metric that no dashboard or alert refers to, because instrumentation libraries often emit dozens of metrics that nobody reads. Recording rules precompute expensive queries on a schedule and store the results as much smaller series, so a dashboard that shows the per-region 99th percentile reads a few precomputed series instead of thousands of raw ones. For older data, Thanos keeps raw samples for 15 days and then downsamples them to five-minute and one-hour resolution, which is still adequate for 30-day indicators.

Logs.

Logs are often the largest telemetry cost, because every event produces a record, and the most effective saving is a record that is never written. At Baodium, load-balancer health checks every few seconds across hundreds of instances were producing millions of access-log lines a day that nobody read, so successful health checks are now excluded from the logs. Debug logging is disabled in production, informational messages written on every request are sampled, and warnings, errors, and business events such as payment attempts are always kept. Logs remain searchable for 14 days and are then archived to object storage, where a year of retention costs little but searches are slow.

Traces.

At its peak of 500 requests per second, with about 12 spans per request, checkout produces 6,000 spans per second. At roughly 1 KB per span, a full day at that rate would produce about 500 GB. The actual daily average is closer to 200 requests per second, or about 200 GB a day, so collectors are sized for the peak while storage costs follow the average.

Sampling reduces this volume by keeping only some traces. The difficulty lies in choosing which ones to keep, because the traces engineers most need are rare, and a random 1 percent sample retains only 1 percent of them. With head sampling, the first service makes the decision when the trace starts and passes it downstream in the traceparent flags. This approach adds almost no overhead, because unsampled requests produce almost no telemetry, but it decides before anyone knows whether the request will be slow or fail. With tail sampling, every service records every span, and the collectors hold the spans until the trace is complete before deciding based on its status, duration, and attributes. Tail sampling can keep every slow or failed trace, but only at the cost of creating, exporting, and buffering every span. It also requires that the services themselves do not sample, because spans that were never recorded cannot be recovered. Checkout uses tail sampling, configured on each gateway collector as shown in Listing Listing.

A trace is kept if any policy matches. Every error, slow request, pending or failed outcome, and retried payment is kept, along with 5 percent of all other traces, which give engineers normal requests to compare against. If about 3 percent of checkouts are slow or failed, the policy keeps roughly 8 percent of traces and reduces stored trace data from about 200 GB to about 16 GB a day.

The values in this configuration are based on per-collector traffic. At peak, the platform as a whole starts about 2,400 traces per second, 500 of them from checkout, and the agents distribute those traces across four gateway collectors, so each collector receives about 600 new traces per second. The 15-second decision_wait covers the slowest checkout, which the 10-second gateway timeout caps, plus the few seconds that agents take to forward spans. At 600 new traces per second, a 15-second wait means that about 9,000 traces are held at once, so num_traces is set to 50,000 to absorb bursts. Because num_traces limits the number of traces rather than the memory they use, the memory_limiter processor bounds memory separately. It refuses new data above its soft limit of 2,800 MiB, which is the 3,500 MiB limit minus the 700 MiB spike allowance, because losing some traces is preferable to a collector that runs out of memory and loses every trace it holds.

Tail sampling across several collectors also requires every span of a trace to reach the same collector, because a collector can evaluate only a trace it has received in full. The agents guarantee this by routing spans through the collector’s load-balancing exporter, with the trace identifier as the routing key. In addition, because the policy keeps every failed trace but only some successful ones, the trace store overstates the error rate. Service indicators must therefore be computed from metrics, which count every request.

SLIs, SLOs, and Outcome Accounting

Everything so far helps an engineer investigate a single incident, but you have probably wondered how many other customers had the same experience without ever contacting support. Answering that question requires measurements that run continuously. A service level indicator, or SLI, is the ratio of good events to eligible events, with both terms precisely defined, and a service level objective, or SLO, is the target for that ratio over a stated period. Expressing reliability as a ratio of events, rather than as average latency or uptime, keeps it tied to what customers experienced. It also lets a team count how many bad events it can afford, which is the basis of the error budgets discussed in the next section.

Response, Status, and Resolution SLIs

To choose indicators, we start with what the customer needs: a prompt answer, a way to check on the order if that answer is lost, and a final outcome within a reasonable time. Each of these can fail while the others continue to work, so checkout has three indicators.

Response indicator.

The fraction of eligible checkout requests for which the gateway returns a confirmation, a business rejection, or a pending response within 3 seconds. Target: 99 percent over 30 days.

Status indicator.

The fraction of authorized status requests for which the gateway returns the operation’s state, with HTTP status 200, within 1 second. The state may come from a cache and lag the committed state by up to 2 seconds, a limit checked separately by sampling. Target: 99.9 percent over 30 days.

Resolution indicator.

The fraction of accepted checkout operations that reach a final outcome (confirmed, rejected, or cancelled) within 15 minutes of acceptance. Operations routed to manual risk review have their own 24-hour deadline. Target: 99.5 percent over 30 days.

The status target is the strictest for two reasons. A status lookup is a simple read that does not depend on the provider, which makes high reliability achievable, and a failed lookup leaves the customer unsure whether they have paid. The three indicators are needed together because each detects a failure that the other two miss. For instance, a pending response returned within 3 seconds satisfies the response indicator even if the operation then remains unresolved for an hour, which only the resolution indicator detects. Likewise, a status endpoint that fails while every operation resolves on time satisfies the resolution indicator, which only the status indicator detects.

Deciding what counts as a good event requires judgment. A provider decline counts as a good response, because the customer receives a clear answer. A generic “try again” page does not, because if the payment may already have gone through, that advice can lead the customer to pay twice. A pending response counts as good only if it tells the customer how to check on the order and its state was saved before the response was sent, because otherwise the customer receives a promise with nothing behind it.

Eligibility and Missing Completions

An indicator can detect only the failures that its denominator includes. For the response indicator, eligible requests are authenticated, well-formed checkout submissions that reach the gateway, and capacity rejections, upstream failures, timeouts, and disconnections after acceptance all count as bad. Malformed requests are excluded, but their count appears on the dashboard so that a sudden increase is noticed.

Where events are counted matters as much as which events are counted. A service that counted its own handler returns would miss requests lost in a process crash, because the counter would be lost with the process. The gateway, by contrast, runs outside that process and records such requests as upstream terminations or timeouts. The gateway can also crash, however, and because checkout and status requests share the same gateway pool, requests lost in that way must be detected from outside, by comparing load-balancer counts with gateway counts every minute, by looking for browser submission reports with no gateway entry, and by running the external probes.

Computing the Indicators

The response indicator comes from the gateway histogram, with the 3-second bucket providing the deadline and the outcome label identifying actionable results, as shown in Listing Listing. The increase(…[30d]) function returns how much each counter grew over 30 days. In practice, however, querying 30 days of raw histogram series is slow, so hourly numerators and denominators are precomputed with recording rules and then summed.

The status indicator uses the same kind of histogram for the status route, status_request_duration_seconds, with a bucket at 1 second. It is measured from real customer requests rather than from probes, because a fault can affect only some operations, such as those with a corrupt cache entry, while a probe against its test order continues to succeed.

An HTTP 200 response can still contain a stale or incorrect state, so correctness is checked separately by sampling. Each status response includes the version of the state it returned, and a consistency checker examines 1 percent of responses. A sampled response counts as correct when a transition with that version exists and records the same state, and when no newer transition was committed more than 2 seconds before the response was served, with both timestamps taken from clocks synchronized to the same time source. You might ask why the checker does not compare each response with the operation’s current state. The state may have changed legitimately after the response was sent, and every such change would then be flagged as an error. The mismatch rate has its own alert and is kept out of the status indicator, because a sample estimates correctness rather than counting every response.

The resolution indicator cannot be derived from request metrics, because its deadline arrives long after the original request has ended, so a background evaluator computes it instead. Every minute, the evaluator selects accepted operations whose deadline has passed, starting from the durable acceptance record introduced in Chapter 3, and looks up when each operation’s final outcome was first committed, because the current state alone would make a late resolution look timely. It then writes one evaluation row per operation, keyed by the operation identifier so that two evaluator workers cannot count the same operation twice, and increments resolution_evaluations_total with a good or bad label. The evaluator also exports the number of operations waiting to be evaluated, because a stalled evaluator would otherwise stop producing bad events at exactly the moment they matter.

Error Budgets and Alerting

An SLO of 99.9 percent allows 0.1 percent of eligible events to be bad. That allowance, the error budget, turns reliability into something a team can spend. For one million status requests in 30 days, the budget is one thousand bad responses, shared by every source of bad events, from failed releases to dependency outages. When most of the budget has been used, the team slows its releases, and when most of it remains, the team can accept more release risk.

To decide when to alert, we need to know how quickly the budget is being spent. That speed is the burn rate, the observed bad-event fraction divided by the allowed fraction.

burn rate=observed bad-event fraction1−SLO target\text{burn rate} = \frac{\text{observed bad-event fraction}} {1-\text{SLO target}}burn rate=1−SLO targetobserved bad-event fraction​

If 1,300 of those million requests are bad, the burn rate is 0.13 percent divided by 0.1 percent, or 1.3. At that rate, the budget runs out after about 23 days instead of lasting the full 30. The window over which the burn rate is measured matters as much as the number itself, because a burn rate over five minutes describes what is happening now, whereas one over 30 days describes whether the objective will be met.

A paging threshold starts with a decision about how much budget the team is willing to lose before waking someone. Baodium chose 2 percent of the 30-day budget in one hour. Because a 30-day window contains 720 hours, spending 2 percent in one hour corresponds to a burn rate of 0.02×720=14.40.02 \times 720 = 14.40.02×720=14.4. The alert in Listing Listing fires when the status burn rate exceeds 14.4 over both the last hour and the last five minutes, provided that the hour contains at least 500 requests.

The one-hour window ensures that about 2 percent of the budget has actually been spent before anyone is paged, and the five-minute window ensures that the problem is still occurring, so the alert clears within minutes of a fix. A fast-burn alert misses slow leaks, however. A service failing at twice its allowed rate never approaches 14.4, yet it exhausts its budget in 15 days. A second alert therefore opens a ticket when the burn rate exceeds 1 over both the last three days and the last six hours.

Low volume and missing data.

Ratios become unreliable when the denominator is small. With twenty status requests in an hour, a single failure is a 5 percent failure rate and a burn rate of 50, so the alert requires at least 500 requests in the hour. Below that volume, a count-based rule applies instead, which opens a ticket after five bad requests in an hour and pages only if an external probe for the same endpoint is also failing. Missing data needs its own alert, because a ratio with an empty denominator has no value, and an alert expression with no value never fires. If the gateway stopped emitting metrics, every burn-rate alert would stop evaluating at the same moment. Separate alerts therefore fire when checkout or status traffic drops to zero during hours that always have traffic, and when absent(status_request_duration_seconds_count) becomes true.

Routing.

A page should tell the responder where to begin. For that reason, each customer-facing alert includes the affected region, the eligible and bad counts, recent deployment versions, and exemplar links to slow traces. Alertmanager groups related alerts, so forty failing instances produce one notification instead of forty, and it routes pages to the on-call engineer and component alerts to a ticket queue.

Measuring Release Impact

The investigation pointed to two delays on the critical path, the payment retry and the connection wait, and the team considered three changes to address them. A shorter payment-attempt timeout would reduce the time spent waiting on unanswered calls, but it would also abandon some attempts that would have succeeded slowly and increase the number of pending operations. Taking the retry out of the request path would shorten responses, but it would shift work to recovery workers whose spare capacity nobody had measured. Releasing the database connection before calling Payment Service, and acquiring a new one to record the result, would remove the cause of the connection wait entirely, so the team started with that change.

Before shipping the change, the team recorded three expectations: what should improve (the 99th percentile of connection wait), what might get worse (database load), and what result would stop the rollout (a response indicator more than 0.2 percentage points below the existing version’s over any hour). Deciding these in advance prevents anyone from reinterpreting the result afterward. The change went first to a 5 percent canary, a small deployment that exposes a new version to real traffic while limiting how many customers a faulty change can affect. The team watched absolute indicator values as well as the gap between the two versions, because a provider slowdown during the canary would affect both versions at once. Connection wait returned to normal even during periods of high provider latency, pending frequency did not change, and the team rolled the change out to every instance.

Testing Monitoring Coverage

Much of your instrumentation code runs only when something fails, which means it rarely runs at all, and a broken timeout handler or disconnect branch can go unnoticed for months. The only reliable way to confirm that a failure will be recorded correctly is to cause it deliberately in a staging environment and examine what the telemetry shows. Baodium runs five such tests on the checkout path.

Provider timeout.

A stub provider delays its first response past the attempt timeout. The payment span must show a timeout rather than a decline, the retry must include the same operation reference, and the reconciliation trace must link back to the checkout trace.

Worker crash.

A worker is terminated immediately after writing the acceptance record, and the operation must still reach the resolution evaluator and be counted as bad when its deadline passes.

Client disconnect.

A test client closes its connection one second into a checkout, and the gateway must record a disconnected outcome rather than a returned response.

Pool exhaustion.

The pool is reduced to one connection, which the test holds open, and the acquisition span must appear before any query span.

Unreadable status.

A committed operation’s cache entry is corrupted so that the status endpoint returns HTTP 500 for that operation alone. The status indicator must count every lookup of that operation as bad, even though the resolution indicator and the external probe report success.

Each test ends with automated queries against the monitoring backend, which allows it to run again after every instrumentation change, and two of the tests have already found real problems. The unreadable-status test showed why the status indicator must be measured from real requests, and the pool-exhaustion test revealed a service whose database client created no acquisition span, which meant that its pool waiting had been reported as query execution.

Field note

Facebook, October 2021

During maintenance on October 4, 2021, a command intended to assess the capacity of Facebook’s backbone network instead cut the connections between its data centers, and an audit tool that should have blocked the command failed because of a bug. Facebook’s DNS servers, which were designed to withdraw their BGP advertisements when they lost contact with the data centers, did exactly that, and the same loss of network access disabled many of the internal tools that engineers would have used for repair. Engineers had to travel to the data centers in person before they could restore service.

Baodium’s telemetry pipeline depends on the same network and identity systems as checkout, so a failure in those systems would also take down the dashboards that the on-call engineer relies on, leaving only the external probes to report. For each tool you would use to diagnose or recover from an outage, list what it depends on, and rehearse a recovery route that still works when that dependency is unavailable.

Summary

The customer’s question about checkout could not be answered from a healthy CPU graph or a successful payment-service counter. The order database established that the order was committed, the gateway recorded how far its response progressed, and browser telemetry could indicate whether the confirmation was displayed. Each record concerned a different measurement boundary. When a record was missing, the engineer had to treat that part of the outcome as unverified.

Metrics identify changes across populations of requests. Traces isolate waiting and execution on a particular request path; logs and durable operation records explain state transitions across retries and recovery. These records become useful together when request, trace, and business-operation identities are propagated consistently and sensitive identifiers are protected. A checkout response indicator alone cannot establish that a pending authorization eventually resolved. Baodium therefore measures response, status-lookup availability, and operation resolution separately, with denominators that account for failures as well as successes.

The strongest monitoring test deliberately produces the outcomes the system must distinguish: a lost response after commit, a blocked request before admission, a delayed provider result, and a missing browser acknowledgement. Operators should be able to reconstruct each case without guessing. Chapter 9 uses the same measurements to choose concurrency limits and decide what happens to requests that the application cannot safely admit.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & Component measurements below their paging thresholds mean checkout is meeting its customer-facing commitments.
Condition that tests it & Requests complete without errors while responses are lost, status lookups fail for some operations, or operations remain unresolved.
Constraint or invariant & Committed state, returned responses, and displayed results are separate observations, and every indicator names its eligible events, point of measurement, and treatment of missing data.
Evidence and uncertainty & Traces and pool metrics separate connection waiting from connection holding, provider records establish how many authorizations occurred, and each known telemetry gap has a detection measurement.
Signal and evaluation window & Burn rate for each indicator over the objective window and the fast-burn and slow-burn windows, with a minimum event count and a missing-data alert.
Control and decision & Page on fast burn, open a ticket on slow burn or a failed component, and treat missing telemetry as an unresolved measurement problem.
Owner and review trigger & The checkout team owns outcome definitions and indicators, and the platform team owns the telemetry pipeline, health checks, and probes. Review after any incident in which requests appeared successful but the customer’s outcome was not, and before expanding a release.
